label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Peter, I take your point about HR becoming the lender of first resort. Your nine years in payroll matter here: you will have seen the repeat requests, the recovery problems and the time spent making exceptions. I also agree that Brenda’s current arrangement needs to change. People coming to her office, explaining their circumstances and getting an advance without a written limit is not a fair or sustainable system.

Where I disagree quite strongly is with “it’s painful for one or two pay cycles and then people adjust”. We tried almost exactly your recommendation in 2025. We eventually reversed it because what happened afterwards was not an improvement, either for staff or for the business.

We have roughly 340 staff in logistics, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. We closed salary advances in February 2025 after Finance raised essentially the same objections: we are not a bank, advances complicate cash flow, and some employees were requesting them every month.

We gave two months’ notice, rather than your suggested three, and held a financial literacy session with the SACCO. We did not just announce it on payday and leave people stranded.

Over the following six months, reception logged **61 debt-collector and loan-app calls to the office**, up from a handful previously. Some apps were contacting supervisors whom employees had listed as “referees”.

Those loans were the employees’ own contracts, certainly. But the consequences did not stay between the employee and the lender. Reception was handling calls. Supervisors were being pulled into collection conversations. HR was dealing with the fallout. Closing our advance window did not remove the work; some of it simply arrived through a different door.

We also saw an increase in unplanned absence on the two days after month-end. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers who were “sorting out” loans.

I would not pretend that this proves every additional absence was caused by stopping advances. It does not. But three missed runs and 61 logged calls are business issues worth putting alongside the cost of administering advances. They cannot sensibly be dismissed as private financial decisions with no workplace consequences.

One loader had six loan apps running at once by the time he came to me, borrowing from one to repay another. It took us four months working with payroll to unwind the situation. That was considerably more HR work than processing a controlled advance would have been.

So, yes, people adjusted. Some adjusted by taking on more expensive and more difficult debt. That is not the same as the underlying problem being solved.

On SACCOs, I am very much in favour. We still encourage staff to use ours. But our SACCO loans take two to three weeks to process and require guarantors. That can work for a planned expense. It is not much help when a child is sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday.

Financial literacy is useful too. I would not drop it. But on KES 28,000 a month, knowing how to budget does not necessarily mean there is enough left to build an emergency fund. There are poor borrowing decisions, and there are genuine gaps between an urgent bill and payday. A policy needs to recognise both.

We reopened advances in September 2025, but we did **not** bring back the old informal arrangement. We introduced a written policy:

- A maximum advance of **40% of net pay**.
- No more than one advance per pay cycle.
- Full repayment through the next payroll.
- No fee.
- Applications through the payroll portal, not a visit to my office.
- A check on existing deductions before approval.

That last point matters. The Employment Act limits total deductions to two-thirds of wages, so we check that separately before approving. The 40% net-pay cap is our policy ceiling, not a substitute for checking the total deductions position. Someone does not automatically qualify for the full 40% if their other deductions make it inappropriate. Nobody is left with nothing at month-end.

Since reopening, we have been handling about 55–70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. Recovery has been 100% apart from two leavers, with roughly KES 14,000 written off for the year.

Your warning about leavers is therefore fair. We have had losses. I would not present the scheme to an MD as risk-free. But I would put the actual write-off figure on the table, rather than treating any possibility of a loss as sufficient reason to close it.

I would also compare that figure, and the administration time, with the cost of absence, missed runs, collection calls and the staff time spent resolving debt problems. The difficulty is that the advance costs are visible in payroll, while the other costs are spread across reception, operations, supervisors and HR. That does not make the latter costs disappear.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. Not because he has decided that the company should become a bank, but because the forecast impact is known in advance. There is a fixed ceiling and a defined process, rather than an open-ended stream of personal requests and exceptions.

That is the distinction I would encourage Brenda to take into her meeting on the 18th: **the choice is not between keeping the informal system unchanged and abolishing advances altogether.**

Peter is right that her current system invites dependency, inconsistent decisions and unnecessary HR administration. But written rules and limits address those problems more directly than assuming every employee will manage better once the window closes.

Brenda, I would go into that meeting acknowledging Finance’s concerns, then propose a controlled policy for a defined trial period. The bones could be the same as ours: a net-pay cap, once per pay cycle, recovery at the next payroll, a formal application and approval route, and checks against existing deductions and the legal limit. The exact cap should be something your payroll and Finance teams can support, not a number adopted just because another employer uses it.

Take whatever numbers you can establish before the meeting:

- How many advances are being requested, and for how much?
- How many people request them repeatedly?
- What is the actual administration time?
- What has been lost through unrecovered balances?
- What cash-flow exposure would a written cap create?
- Are reception, supervisors or operations already dealing with debt-related disruption?

Then agree what you will measure during the trial and when you will review it. Repeated monthly requests deserve attention, but they are also information about affordability; they should not simply trigger another lecture or an automatic exception.

Peter, I agree with you that HR should not spend its days lending money and hearing individual appeals. That is one reason I prefer a portal and clear rules. Where our experience differs is the assumption that shutting the scheme ends the company’s involvement. For us, it ended the controlled part of our involvement and left us handling consequences we had not properly costed.

Brenda’s instinct needs numbers behind it. Finance’s proposal deserves the same scrutiny. We tried closure, recorded what followed, and found that a limited, predictable advance scheme was the more workable option.
